fields.Question:
One pass Two Sum stores value to index in a dict. Which loop body is correct on every input, including nums = [3, 4], target = 6, which has no valid pair?
for i, x in enumerate(nums):
    # body
fields.Choices:
Check x in seen, then set seen[target - x] = i only when x is even
Sort nums first, then check target - x in seen
Check target - x in seen, then set seen[x] = i
Set seen[x] = i, then check target - x in seen
fields.Correct: Check target - x in seen, then set seen[x] = i
fields.Explanation: Checking before inserting guarantees an element never pairs with itself. Inserting first finds 3 when x = 3 and returns [0, 0]. The even parity rule is arbitrary and breaks normal inputs. Sorting loses the original indices and adds O(n log n) for nothing.

fields.Question: Group anagrams over n lowercase words of max length k. Which key gives O(n k) total time?
fields.Choices:
A set of the word's characters
A tuple of 26 letter counts
The sorted word
The sum of character codes
fields.Correct: A tuple of 26 letter counts
fields.Explanation: A count tuple is built in O(k) and identifies the letter multiset exactly. Sorting each word costs O(k log k), correct but slower. A character code sum collides ("ad" and "bc"). A set drops multiplicity, so "aab" and "abb" collide.
fields.Hint: The key must be exact and linear in word length.

fields.Question: Return true if any value appears at least twice in nums, n up to 10^5, values any 32 bit integer. Which approach is O(n) expected time?
fields.Choices:
Compare every pair
Insert into a hash set and stop on the first repeat
Sort and compare neighbours
A boolean array indexed by value
fields.Correct: Insert into a hash set and stop on the first repeat
fields.Explanation: A hash set gives O(1) expected insert and lookup. Sorting works but is O(n log n). A boolean array indexed by value needs 2^32 slots and fails on negatives. Comparing every pair is O(n^2).
fields.Hint: Values span the full integer range.

fields.Question: Longest Consecutive Sequence must run in O(n). You put all values in a set. Which rule keeps the total work O(n)?
fields.Choices:
Sort the set and count runs
Only start counting from x when x + 1 is not in the set and count upward
Only start counting from x when x - 1 is not in the set
Start counting from every x in the set
fields.Correct: Only start counting from x when x - 1 is not in the set
fields.Explanation: Starting only at run beginnings means each value is visited by one count walk, so the total is O(n). Starting from every x is O(n^2) on one long run. Sorting is O(n log n). Starting where x + 1 is missing marks run ends, so counting upward from there finds nothing; the rule must match the direction you walk.
fields.Hint: Each run should be walked once.

fields.Question: Top K Frequent Elements, n up to 10^5, any k. Which method is O(n) time?
fields.Choices:
Count, then call max() k times on the counts
Count with a dict, then bucket values by frequency in a list of size n + 1
Count, then sort the items by frequency
Count, then keep a size k min heap
fields.Correct: Count with a dict, then bucket values by frequency in a list of size n + 1
fields.Explanation: Frequencies are bounded by n, so bucketing by frequency is O(n). Sorting is O(n log n). A size k heap is O(n log k), good but not O(n) for large k. Calling max k times is O(n k).

fields.Question: Check whether t is an anagram of s where both may contain any Unicode characters. Which is correct and O(n)?
fields.Choices:
Compare sum(map(ord, s)) == sum(map(ord, t))
Compare Counter(s) == Counter(t)
Use a 26 slot count array
Compare set(s) == set(t)
fields.Correct: Compare Counter(s) == Counter(t)
fields.Explanation: Counter keys by any character and compares multiplicities. A 26 slot array assumes lowercase ASCII and breaks on other characters. Sets ignore counts. Ord sums collide for different strings.

fields.Question: In CPython, what is the worst case time of a single dict lookup?
fields.Choices:
O(n)
O(1)
O(log n)
O(n log n)
fields.Correct: O(n)
fields.Explanation: Average is O(1), but if many keys collide the probe sequence can touch O(n) entries, which the Python wiki lists as the amortized worst case. O(1) is the average, not the worst. O(log n) is a balanced tree, which dict is not. O(n log n) has no basis for one lookup.
fields.Hint: Average and worst differ for hash tables.

fields.Question: You want to memoize on a list argument in Python. Which key works as a dict key?
fields.Choices:
lst
set(lst)
[tuple(lst)]
tuple(lst)
fields.Correct: tuple(lst)
fields.Explanation: Tuples of hashable items are hashable. A list is mutable and raises TypeError. A set is unhashable and also drops order and duplicates. Wrapping in a list is still a list.

fields.Question: Isomorphic strings: s = "badc", t = "baba". A solution maps each char of s to t with one dict and returns True. What did it miss?
fields.Choices:
It should compare lengths only
It should sort both strings
Nothing, the answer True is correct
It never checks the reverse mapping, so two s chars map to the same t char
fields.Correct: It never checks the reverse mapping, so two s chars map to the same t char
fields.Explanation: Isomorphism needs a bijection. The forward map b to b, a to a, d to b, c to a is consistent, but b and d both map to b, so the answer is False and a reverse dict (or a set of used targets) is required. Equal lengths say nothing about structure. Sorting destroys positions. True is wrong because t reuses b for two different s letters.
fields.Hint: Two different letters cannot share an image.

fields.Question: Ransom note: can note be built from the letters in magazine, each letter used once? Give the approach and complexity.
fields.Answer: Count magazine letters with a Counter, then decrement for each note letter and fail when a count goes below zero. O(m + n) time, O(alphabet) space. Pitfall: checking membership only, not counts, accepts "aa" from "a".

fields.Question: Two Sum on an unsorted array, return indices. A candidate proposes left and right pointers moving inward. What is wrong?
fields.Choices:
It is O(n^2)
It needs a hash set of visited pointers
Pointer moves are only valid on sorted input, and sorting loses the original indices
Nothing, two pointers works on any array
fields.Correct: Pointer moves are only valid on sorted input, and sorting loses the original indices
fields.Explanation: Moving left up when the sum is too small relies on sorted order. Without sorting the moves skip valid pairs, and sorting needs index tracking. It is not O(n^2), it is wrong. A visited set of pointers fixes nothing.
fields.Hint: Why does moving left increase the sum?

fields.Question: 3Sum on sorted nums must return unique triplets. After finding a triplet at (i, l, r), what avoids duplicates without a set?
fields.Choices:
Only skip i when nums[i] equals nums[i + 1] before using it
Break out of the inner loop after the first triplet
Remove duplicates from nums before the loop
Advance l while nums[l] equals the previous value, and skip i when nums[i] equals nums[i - 1]
fields.Correct: Advance l while nums[l] equals the previous value, and skip i when nums[i] equals nums[i - 1]
fields.Explanation: Skipping equal neighbours for both the anchor and the inner pointer removes repeats while keeping valid triplets. Skipping i against i + 1 drops the first copy and loses triplets like [-1, -1, 2]. Breaking after one triplet misses others with the same anchor. Deduplicating the input loses triplets that need repeated values such as [0, 0, 0].
fields.Hint: Duplicates come from both the anchor and the pair.

fields.Question: Container With Most Water uses two pointers. Which pointer moves each step?
fields.Choices:
The one with the taller line
Both pointers every step
The left one always
The one with the shorter line
fields.Correct: The one with the shorter line
fields.Explanation: Area is limited by the shorter line, and any container keeping that short line with a narrower width cannot be larger, so discarding it is safe. Moving the taller line can only keep or reduce height while width shrinks. Moving both can skip the optimum. Always moving left ignores heights entirely.

fields.Question: Valid Palindrome ignoring non alphanumeric characters and case. Which is O(1) extra space?
fields.Choices:
Use a stack of all alphanumeric chars
Recursively strip the ends
Two pointers from both ends, skipping non alphanumerics and comparing lowercased chars
Build a filtered string and compare it to its reverse
fields.Correct: Two pointers from both ends, skipping non alphanumerics and comparing lowercased chars
fields.Explanation: Inward pointers use constant space. Building a filtered copy is O(n) space. A stack is O(n). Recursive stripping creates new strings and uses O(n) stack.
fields.Hint: Do not build a new string.

fields.Choices:
Wrong, it should compare nums[i] with nums[i + 1]
Wrong, k must start at 0
Wrong, it needs a hash set
Correct as written for non empty input
fields.Correct: Correct as written for non empty input
fields.Explanation: The write pointer k compares against the last kept value, which is right for any non empty sorted array (empty input needs a guard). Comparing i with i + 1 reads past the end. Starting k at 0 makes nums[k - 1] read the last element. A hash set is unnecessary when input is sorted.
fields.Hint: Compare against the last written value.
fields.Source: LeetCode 26. Remove Duplicates from Sorted Array (https://leetcode.com/problems/remove-duplicates-from-sorted-array/)

fields.Question: Move Zeroes keeps non zero order and runs in place. What is the time complexity of the swap based write pointer method?
fields.Choices:
O(n)
O(n log n)
O(n^2)
O(k n) for k zeroes
fields.Correct: O(n)
fields.Explanation: Each element is read once and swapped at most once. O(n log n) would need sorting, which also breaks order. O(n^2) is shifting elements left for every zero. O(k n) is the same naive shift counted per zero.
fields.Hint: One pass with a write index.

fields.Question: Trapping Rain Water with two pointers and running left_max and right_max. When height[l] < height[r], what is added at l?
fields.Choices:
left_max - height[l] after updating left_max
right_max - height[l]
min(left_max, right_max) - height[l] computed with right_max from the full array
height[r] - height[l]
fields.Correct: left_max - height[l] after updating left_max
fields.Explanation: When height[l] < height[r], the right side has a wall at least as tall as left_max, so left_max bounds the water at l. Using right_max overcounts when right_max is larger than left_max. Using a precomputed full right_max is the prefix array approach, not this one, and mixing them is inconsistent. height[r] minus height[l] ignores walls between.

fields.Question: Squares of a sorted array that contains negatives, return sorted squares in O(n). How?
fields.Answer: Two pointers at both ends. The largest square is at one end, so compare abs values, write the bigger square to the back of the output, and move that pointer. Pitfall: squaring then sorting is O(n log n).
fields.Hint: The biggest square is at an end.
fields.Source: LeetCode 977. Squares of a Sorted Array (https://leetcode.com/problems/squares-of-a-sorted-array/)

fields.Question: Count subarrays with sum exactly k. nums may contain negative numbers. Which approach is correct in O(n)?
fields.Choices:
Sort, then two pointers
Prefix sums with a hash map of prefix counts
Variable sliding window that shrinks while sum > k
Fixed window of size k
fields.Correct: Prefix sums with a hash map of prefix counts
fields.Explanation: With negatives, extending a window can lower the sum, so the shrink rule is not monotonic and a window misses answers. Counting earlier prefixes equal to prefix minus k handles any values. A fixed size k window confuses the target with a length. Sorting destroys contiguity.
fields.Hint: Is window sum monotonic with negatives?

fields.Question:
Longest substring without repeating characters. Which shrink step is right?
for r, ch in enumerate(s):
    count[ch] += 1
    # shrink here
    best = max(best, r - l + 1)
fields.Choices:
if count[ch] > 1: count[s[l]] -= 1; l += 1
l = r
while count[ch] > 1: l += 1
while count[ch] > 1: count[s[l]] -= 1; l += 1
fields.Correct: while count[ch] > 1: count[s[l]] -= 1; l += 1
fields.Explanation: The window is valid only after the duplicate of ch leaves, which can take several steps, so it must be while. A single if step leaves a duplicate in the window for inputs like "abcb". Setting l = r discards valid characters and leaves stale counts, so later windows are judged wrong. Moving l without decrementing counts never clears the duplicate and loops forever.
fields.Hint: One step may not be enough.
fields.Source: LeetCode 3. Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters (https://leetcode.com/problems/longest-substring-without-repeating-characters/)

fields.Question: Minimum Window Substring over s of length m and t of length n with a need counter. What is the time complexity?
fields.Choices:
O(m + n)
O(m n)
O(m^2)
O(m log m)
fields.Correct: O(m + n)
fields.Explanation: Each index of s enters and leaves the window at most once, and building the need counter costs O(n). O(m n) assumes rechecking all of t per step, which a formed counter avoids. O(m^2) is trying every start. Nothing is sorted, so no log factor.

fields.Question: Longest Repeating Character Replacement with at most k changes. When is the window [l, r] invalid?
fields.Choices:
number of distinct chars > k
(r - l + 1) - max_count > k
max_count > k
(r - l + 1) > k
fields.Correct: (r - l + 1) - max_count > k
fields.Explanation: The cells not equal to the majority letter must be replaced, which is window length minus max_count, and that must be at most k. max_count above k is fine because those letters need no change. Length above k ignores the majority. Distinct letters do not count replacements; "aab" has 2 distinct but needs 1 change.
fields.Hint: What must you change in the window?

fields.Question: Max average of a contiguous subarray of length exactly k, n up to 10^5. What is the best time?
fields.Choices:
O(n) with a monotonic deque
O(n) with a running window sum
O(n k) recomputing each window
O(n log n) with sorting
fields.Correct: O(n) with a running window sum
fields.Explanation: Add the entering value and subtract the leaving one: O(n). Recomputing is O(n k). Sorting breaks contiguity. A monotonic deque is O(n) too but solves window max, not sum, so it is the wrong tool here.

fields.Question: Does s2 contain a permutation of s1, lowercase letters? Which window works?
fields.Choices:
Variable window that grows until it contains every letter of s1
Sort every substring of s2 of length len(s1)
Check whether set(s1) is a subset of set(s2)
Fixed window of len(s1) with 26 counts, compare on each slide
fields.Correct: Fixed window of len(s1) with 26 counts, compare on each slide
fields.Explanation: A permutation has exactly len(s1) characters, so a fixed window with count compare is O(26 n). A growing variable window can contain extra letters and still pass. Sorting every window is O(n k log k). The set check ignores counts and contiguity.
fields.Hint: A permutation has a known length.

fields.Question: Minimum Size Subarray Sum: positive integers, find the shortest subarray with sum >= target. Why is a sliding window valid here?
fields.Choices:
All values are positive, so shrinking always decreases the sum
Because the array is sorted
Because target is positive
It is not valid, prefix sums are required
fields.Correct: All values are positive, so shrinking always decreases the sum
fields.Explanation: Positivity makes the window sum monotonic in both pointers, so greedy shrinking is safe. The array is not sorted. A positive target alone does not help if values can be negative. Prefix sums with binary search also work in O(n log n), but the window is valid and O(n).

fields.Question: Max Consecutive Ones III: binary array, flip at most k zeros. Approach?
fields.Answer: Variable window counting zeros. Extend r, and while zeros > k move l and decrement zeros when leaving a zero. Track max length. O(n) time, O(1) space. Pitfall: using if instead of while.

fields.Question: Subarray Sum Equals K with a prefix count map. Why initialize counts = {0: 1}?
fields.Choices:
So subarrays that start at index 0 are counted
To avoid a KeyError on the first lookup
Because k is never 0
It is not needed with defaultdict
fields.Correct: So subarrays that start at index 0 are counted
fields.Explanation: A prefix equal to k means the whole prefix is a valid subarray, which needs an empty prefix of sum 0 counted once. A KeyError is avoided by get, not by seeding. k can be 0. defaultdict defaults missing keys to 0, which still misses the empty prefix.

fields.Question: Many range sum queries on a fixed array. With P[0] = 0 and P[i + 1] = P[i] + a[i], what is sum(a[l..r]) inclusive?
fields.Explanation: P[r + 1] covers a[0..r] and P[l] covers a[0..l-1]. P[r] minus P[l] drops a[r]. P[r] minus P[l - 1] uses the other indexing convention and fails at l = 0. P[r + 1] minus P[l + 1] drops a[l].

fields.Question: Product of Array Except Self without division in O(n). nums may contain zeros. Which works?
fields.Choices:
Total product divided by nums[i]
Sort, then multiply neighbours
Nested loop skipping i
Left prefix products times right suffix products
fields.Correct: Left prefix products times right suffix products
fields.Explanation: Prefix and suffix products avoid division and handle zeros. Division is banned and fails on zero. Sorting loses positions. The nested loop is O(n^2).
fields.Source: LeetCode 238. Product of Array Except Self (https://leetcode.com/problems/product-of-array-except-self/)

fields.Question: Contiguous Array: longest subarray with equal 0s and 1s. What do you store in the hash map?
fields.Choices:
Count of each balance
Index of each 0
First index where each running balance (+1 for 1, -1 for 0) appears
Last index of each balance
fields.Correct: First index where each running balance (+1 for 1, -1 for 0) appears
fields.Explanation: Equal balances at i and j mean the subarray between is balanced, and the earliest i gives the longest. Storing the last index shortens results. Counts answer how many, not how long. Indices of zeros alone ignore ones.

fields.Question:
Iterative reversal of a singly linked list. Which body is correct?
prev, cur = None, head
while cur:
    # body
return prev
fields.Choices:
nxt = cur.next; prev = cur; cur.next = prev; cur = nxt
nxt = cur.next; cur.next = prev; prev = cur; cur = nxt
cur.next = prev; prev = cur; cur = cur.next
prev = cur; cur.next = prev; cur = cur.next
fields.Correct: nxt = cur.next; cur.next = prev; prev = cur; cur = nxt
fields.Explanation: Save next before overwriting it, then link back and advance. Overwriting cur.next first makes cur = cur.next jump to prev and loses the rest. Setting prev before relinking makes cur point to itself. The last option also links cur to itself because prev was already moved.

fields.Question: Detect a cycle in O(1) space. Which is right?
fields.Choices:
Count steps and stop after 10^4
Store visited nodes in a set
Fast moves two, slow moves one; a cycle exists if they meet
Mark nodes by setting node.val = None
fields.Correct: Fast moves two, slow moves one; a cycle exists if they meet
fields.Explanation: Floyd's tortoise and hare meets inside any cycle and uses O(1) space. Mutating values corrupts input and fails if None is a valid value. A step cap is a guess tied to constraints. A visited set is correct but O(n) space.

fields.Question: Remove the nth node from the end in one pass, where n can equal the list length. What avoids a special case for removing the head?
fields.Choices:
Reverse the list first
Compute the length, then walk again
A dummy node before head, with both pointers starting at it
Start both pointers at head
fields.Correct: A dummy node before head, with both pointers starting at it
fields.Explanation: With a dummy, the slow pointer lands on the node before the target even when the target is the head. Starting at head needs a separate branch for n equal to length. Reversing is extra passes and still has edge cases. Length then walk is two passes, not one.
fields.Source: LeetCode 19. Remove Nth Node From End of List (https://leetcode.com/problems/remove-nth-node-from-end-of-list/)

fields.Question: Merge two sorted lists of lengths m and n. What is the time and extra space of the iterative merge?
fields.Choices:
O(m + n) time, O(1) extra space
O(m + n) time, O(m + n) extra space
O(m n) time, O(1) space
O((m + n) log(m + n)) time
fields.Correct: O(m + n) time, O(1) extra space
fields.Explanation: Relinking existing nodes behind a dummy needs only pointers. Extra O(m + n) space is the recursive version's stack or copying into new nodes. O(m n) is inserting each node by scanning. Sorting the union adds an unnecessary log factor.

fields.Question: Middle of the Linked List: return the second middle when length is even. Loop: while fast and fast.next: slow, fast = slow.next, fast.next.next. Both start at head. What does it return for 1->2->3->4?
fields.Choices:
Node 3
Node 2
Node 4
It raises on fast.next.next
fields.Correct: Node 3
fields.Explanation: For 4 nodes, slow moves twice to node 3, which is the second middle. Node 2 is what you get if fast starts at head.next. Node 4 is the tail. The guard checks fast.next before reading fast.next.next, so nothing raises.
fields.Source: LeetCode 876. Middle of the Linked List (https://leetcode.com/problems/middle-of-the-linked-list/)

fields.Question: Reorder List L0, Ln, L1, Ln-1 in place with O(1) extra space. Approach?
fields.Answer: Find the middle with slow and fast, reverse the second half, then merge the two halves alternately. Cut the first half at the middle to avoid a cycle. O(n) time, O(1) space.

fields.Question: Rotate an n x n matrix 90 degrees clockwise in place. Which works?
fields.Choices:
Reverse each row, then transpose
Transpose, then reverse each column
Swap matrix[i][j] with matrix[j][i] for all i and j
Transpose, then reverse each row
fields.Correct: Transpose, then reverse each row
fields.Explanation: Transpose plus row reverse is clockwise. Row reverse then transpose gives counterclockwise. Transpose plus column reverse is also counterclockwise. Swapping over all i and j swaps every pair twice and returns the original.

fields.Question: Set Matrix Zeroes in O(1) extra space using the first row and column as markers. What extra state is needed?
fields.Choices:
One flag for whether the first column (or row) itself had a zero
Nothing extra
A set of zero rows
A copy of the first row
fields.Correct: One flag for whether the first column (or row) itself had a zero
fields.Explanation: matrix[0][0] can mark only one of row 0 or column 0, so one more flag is needed for the other. Without it, row 0 or column 0 is wrongly zeroed or missed. A set of rows is O(m) space. Copying the first row is O(n) space.

fields.Question: Spiral Matrix on a 3 x 1 matrix. A boundary loop goes right, down, left, up and shrinks top, right, bottom, left. What bug outputs some cells twice?
fields.Choices:
Shrinking top after the right pass
Using range(left, right + 1)
Starting at matrix[0][0]
Not checking top <= bottom and left <= right before the left and up passes
fields.Correct: Not checking top <= bottom and left <= right before the left and up passes
fields.Explanation: For single row or column leftovers, the left and up passes revisit cells unless guarded. Shrinking top after the right pass is correct. Inclusive ranges are correct with inclusive bounds. Starting at [0][0] is correct.

fields.Question: Search a 2D Matrix where each row is sorted and each row's first value exceeds the previous row's last. Best time?
fields.Choices:
O(log(m n)) treating it as one sorted array
O(m + n) staircase from the top right
O(m log n) binary search each row
O(m n)
fields.Correct: O(log(m n)) treating it as one sorted array
fields.Explanation: The global ordering makes it a flat sorted array of m n cells, so one binary search works. The staircase is O(m + n), correct but slower and meant for the weaker ordering of LeetCode 240. Per row search ignores the cross row order. Scanning is O(m n).

fields.Question: Valid Sudoku: which index gives the 3 x 3 box of cell (r, c)?
fields.Explanation: Row band times 3 plus column band gives 0 to 8. r // 3 + c // 3 collides (band 0,1 and 1,0). The modulo version gives position within a box, not the box. r * 3 + c is out of range.

fields.Question: Grid BFS for shortest path, 1000 x 1000 open grid. The code marks a cell visited when it is popped. What happens?
fields.Choices:
It turns into DFS
Cells are enqueued many times, blowing up time and memory
Distances become wrong but runtime is fine
Nothing, it is equivalent to marking on push
fields.Correct: Cells are enqueued many times, blowing up time and memory
fields.Explanation: Until a cell is popped, every neighbour that sees it pushes another copy, so the queue holds many duplicates and often times out. The first pop still has the right distance, so results are correct but slow. It is not equivalent to marking on push. The queue is still FIFO, so it is not DFS.
fields.Hint: When does a cell stop being re-added?
fields.Source: LeetCode 1091. Shortest Path in Binary Matrix (https://leetcode.com/problems/shortest-path-in-binary-matrix/)

fields.Question: Shortest path by edge count in an unweighted graph. Which is correct and fastest?
fields.Choices:
Dijkstra with a heap, O((V + E) log V)
Bellman Ford, O(V E)
BFS, O(V + E)
DFS, keeping the min depth seen
fields.Correct: BFS, O(V + E)
fields.Explanation: BFS explores in distance order, so the first visit is shortest. Plain DFS with a visited set can reach a node by a long path first and never revisit it. Dijkstra is correct but adds a log factor for no reason. Bellman Ford is correct and much slower.

fields.Question: Number of Islands on an m x n grid with DFS. What is the time complexity?
fields.Choices:
O(m n log(m n))
O(m n)
O((m n)^2)
O(m + n)
fields.Correct: O(m n)
fields.Explanation: Each cell is visited a constant number of times, with 4 neighbour checks. Squaring the cell count treats it like a dense graph. O(m + n) counts rows and columns, not cells. There is no sorting or heap.
fields.Hint: V is the number of cells, E is about 4V.

fields.Question: Python recursive DFS on a 1000 x 1000 grid that is one big island. What goes wrong?
fields.Choices:
Infinite loop
Nothing, Python grows the stack
RecursionError, since depth can reach about 10^6 and the default limit is 1000
Wrong island count
fields.Correct: RecursionError, since depth can reach about 10^6 and the default limit is 1000
fields.Explanation: CPython's default recursion limit is about 1000 frames, and a snake shaped island can make DFS depth near the cell count. Use an explicit stack or BFS. The count would be right if it finished. Visited marking prevents infinite loops. Python does not grow the stack automatically.

fields.Question: Rotting Oranges: every rotten orange spreads each minute. How do you get the minimum minutes?
fields.Choices:
Push all rotten oranges into the queue first, then BFS by levels
Run BFS from each rotten orange and take the min per cell
DFS from each rotten orange
Simulate minute by minute rescanning the whole grid
fields.Correct: Push all rotten oranges into the queue first, then BFS by levels
fields.Explanation: Multi source BFS gives each cell its distance to the nearest source in O(m n). One BFS per source is O(k m n). DFS does not give shortest distances. Full rescans are O((m n)^2) in the worst case.

fields.Question: Clone Graph with a cycle. What prevents infinite recursion and duplicate clones?
fields.Choices:
A visited set of node values only, without storing clones
Cloning neighbours before the node itself
Limiting depth to the node count
A dict from original node to its clone, checked before creating
fields.Correct: A dict from original node to its clone, checked before creating
fields.Explanation: The map both marks visited and returns the existing clone so edges point to one copy. A set of values knows a node was seen but cannot hand back its clone, so edges cannot be wired. Cloning neighbours first still recurses forever on a cycle. Depth limits produce partial copies.
fields.Hint: You need the clone, not just a flag.

fields.Question: Binary tree level order traversal with a deque. How do you separate levels?
fields.Choices:
Push a None after every node
Use a stack instead of a queue
Track depth with a global counter incremented on each pop
Record len(queue) at the start of each level and pop exactly that many
fields.Correct: Record len(queue) at the start of each level and pop exactly that many
fields.Explanation: The queue length at the start of a level equals that level's node count. A None after every node splits per node, not per level. A stack gives DFS order. Incrementing per pop counts nodes, not levels.
fields.Source: LeetCode 102. Binary Tree Level Order Traversal (https://leetcode.com/problems/binary-tree-level-order-traversal/)

fields.Question: Pacific Atlantic Water Flow on m x n. Which is O(m n)?
fields.Choices:
DFS from every cell checking if it reaches both oceans
Sort cells by height and sweep
Dijkstra from each border cell
BFS or DFS inward from each ocean's border going uphill, then intersect
fields.Correct: BFS or DFS inward from each ocean's border going uphill, then intersect
fields.Explanation: Reversing the flow lets two searches cover all cells once each. Per cell DFS is O((m n)^2). Sorting is O(m n log(m n)) and does not by itself decide reachability. Dijkstra adds weights that do not exist.

fields.Question: Surrounded Regions: flip O regions not connected to the border. What is the clean approach?
fields.Choices:
Flip every O, then restore ones on the border only
DFS from each interior O and flip if it does not hit the border, without marking
Union find of all O cells without a border sentinel
Mark border connected O cells first, then flip all unmarked O
fields.Correct: Mark border connected O cells first, then flip all unmarked O
fields.Explanation: Marking from the border first identifies safe cells in O(m n). Restoring only border cells forgets interior cells connected to them. Unmarked per cell DFS repeats work and is O((m n)^2). Union find works only with a virtual border node; without one you cannot tell which components touch the edge.

fields.Question: Undirected graph from an edge list, n up to 10^5. Which representation fits BFS in O(V + E)?
fields.Choices:
Adjacency matrix
Adjacency list adding each edge once from u to v
Edge list scanned per node
Adjacency list, adding each edge in both directions
fields.Correct: Adjacency list, adding each edge in both directions
fields.Explanation: An adjacency list stores E entries and both directions are needed for undirected edges. A matrix is 10^10 cells. One direction only makes v unable to reach u. Scanning the edge list per node is O(V E).

fields.Question: Word Ladder: word length L, dictionary size N. Which neighbour generation is usually fastest when N is large?
fields.Choices:
For each position, try all 26 letters and check a word set, O(26 L) per word
Compare against every dictionary word for one letter difference
Precompute all pairs differing by one letter
DFS through the dictionary
fields.Correct: For each position, try all 26 letters and check a word set, O(26 L) per word
fields.Explanation: Generating candidates costs O(26 L) lookups (each O(L) to hash) independent of N. Comparing to every word is O(N L) per node. All pairs is O(N^2 L). DFS does not give the shortest transformation.

fields.Question: Flood Fill: what edge case makes a naive DFS loop forever, and how do you guard it?
fields.Answer: If the new color equals the starting color, recoloring does not mark cells, so DFS revisits them forever. Return immediately when image[sr][sc] already equals color, or use a visited set.

fields.Question:
Find the first index with nums[i] >= x.
lo, hi = 0, len(nums)
while lo <= hi:
    mid = (lo + hi) // 2
    if nums[mid] >= x: hi = mid
    else: lo = mid + 1
fields.Choices:
hi should start at len(nums) - 1
It can loop forever, the condition should be lo < hi
It is correct
It returns one past the answer
fields.Correct: It can loop forever, the condition should be lo < hi
fields.Explanation: With hi = mid, the half open template needs lo < hi; with lo <= hi, once lo == hi == mid the loop never ends, and mid can also index len(nums). It is not correct. When it does finish lo is the right answer, so it is not off by one. hi = len - 1 breaks the case where no element is >= x.

fields.Question: In Java with int indices up to 2^31 - 1, why write mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2?
fields.Choices:
It rounds up instead of down
It is faster
It avoids an off by one with even lengths
lo + hi can overflow and go negative
fields.Correct: lo + hi can overflow and go negative
fields.Explanation: lo + hi above 2^31 - 1 wraps negative, the bug Joshua Bloch described in the JDK. Both forms round toward zero for non negative values. Speed is the same. Even lengths are not the issue.
fields.Source: Extra, Extra: Nearly All Binary Searches and Mergesorts are Broken (https://research.google/blog/extra-extra-read-all-about-it-nearly-all-binary-searches-and-mergesorts-are-broken/)

fields.Question: Search in Rotated Sorted Array with distinct values. After computing mid, what tells you which half is sorted?
fields.Choices:
nums[mid] < target means the right half is sorted
nums[mid] > nums[hi] means the left half is unsorted
Compare target to nums[0] only
nums[lo] <= nums[mid] means the left half is sorted
fields.Correct: nums[lo] <= nums[mid] means the left half is sorted
fields.Explanation: With distinct values, if nums[lo] <= nums[mid] the left part has no rotation point, and you check whether target falls in it. Comparing mid to target says nothing about where the rotation is. nums[mid] > nums[hi] means the right half holds the rotation, so the left is sorted, the opposite of the claim. Comparing only to nums[0] needs a separate pivot search to be correct.
fields.Source: LeetCode 33. Search in Rotated Sorted Array (https://leetcode.com/problems/search-in-rotated-sorted-array/)

fields.Question: nums = [1, 2, 2, 2, 3]. What does bisect.bisect_left(nums, 2) return?
fields.Explanation: bisect_left returns the leftmost insertion point, index 1. 4 is bisect_right. 3 is the last 2's index. 2 is the middle.

fields.Question: Count occurrences of x in a sorted array of n values. Best time?
fields.Choices:
O(log n + k) finding one then expanding
O(1) with a precomputed array
O(log n) with bisect_right minus bisect_left
O(n) by scanning
fields.Correct: O(log n) with bisect_right minus bisect_left
fields.Explanation: Two binary searches give the range bounds in O(log n). Scanning is O(n). Finding one then expanding is O(log n + k), which degrades to O(n) when x repeats. Precomputing is O(n) setup and not given.

fields.Question: Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array, distinct values. Loop while lo < hi. Which comparison is right?
fields.Choices:
if nums[mid] < nums[hi]: lo = mid + 1 else: hi = mid
if nums[mid] > nums[hi]: lo = mid else: hi = mid - 1
if nums[mid] > nums[hi]: lo = mid + 1 else: hi = mid
if nums[mid] > nums[lo]: lo = mid + 1 else: hi = mid
fields.Correct: if nums[mid] > nums[hi]: lo = mid + 1 else: hi = mid
fields.Explanation: If mid is above hi the minimum is to the right, else mid could be it so keep it. Comparing with lo fails on a non rotated array (it moves past index 0). The flipped comparison walks away from the min. lo = mid with lo < hi can loop forever and hi = mid - 1 can skip the min.
fields.Source: LeetCode 153. Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array (https://leetcode.com/problems/find-minimum-in-rotated-sorted-array/)

fields.Question: Valid Parentheses for s = "(]" and s = "((". Which check is complete?
fields.Choices:
Check that s equals its reverse with brackets flipped
Match each closer to the stack top and return True only if the stack is empty at the end
Count opens and closes of each type
Match each closer to the stack top and return True if no mismatch occurred
fields.Correct: Match each closer to the stack top and return True only if the stack is empty at the end
fields.Explanation: Both conditions matter: "(]" mismatches and "((" leaves items on the stack. Counting types accepts "([)]". Skipping the final empty check accepts "((". The mirror check rejects valid strings like "()()".

fields.Question: Min Stack with O(1) getMin. What do you store?
fields.Choices:
Only the global min, updated on push
A sorted list of all values
A heap of all values
Each entry as (value, min so far)
fields.Correct: Each entry as (value, min so far)
fields.Explanation: Storing the min so far with each entry restores the previous min on pop. A single global min is lost when that min is popped. A sorted list makes push O(n). A heap gives O(log n) push and cannot delete the popped value efficiently.
fields.Hint: What happens after popping the min?

fields.Question: Daily Temperatures, n up to 10^5. What does the monotonic stack hold and what is the time?
fields.Choices:
Indices with decreasing temperatures, O(n)
Temperatures in increasing order, O(n log n)
Indices with increasing temperatures, O(n)
All later indices per day, O(n^2)
fields.Correct: Indices with decreasing temperatures, O(n)
fields.Explanation: Indices of days still waiting for a warmer day form a decreasing stack, and each is pushed and popped once. Values alone lose the distance, and there is no log factor. An increasing stack answers the previous smaller element, not the next warmer one. Scanning all later days is the brute force.

fields.Question: Evaluate Reverse Polish Notation ["4","13","5","/","+"] where division truncates toward zero. In Python, which division is right for negative operands?
fields.Choices:
math.floor(a / b)
int(a / b)
a // b
round(a / b)
fields.Correct: int(a / b)
fields.Explanation: int(a / b) truncates toward zero, matching the spec, for operands in the given range. a // b floors, so -7 // 2 is -4 instead of -3. round rounds to nearest. floor is the same as //. Also pop b before a.
fields.Hint: Floor and truncate differ on negatives.

fields.Question: Queue using two stacks (in and out). When do you move items to out?
fields.Choices:
Only when out is empty, then move all of in
On every pop
On every push
When in has more than one item
fields.Correct: Only when out is empty, then move all of in
fields.Explanation: Moving only when out is empty keeps FIFO order and makes each item move once, so operations are amortized O(1). Moving on every pop is O(n) per pop and breaks order if out is not empty. Moving on push reverses order each time. A size threshold mixes orders.

fields.Question: Decode String such as "3[a2[c]]" to "accaccacc". Approach?
fields.Answer: Stack of (previous string, repeat count). On a digit build the number (it can be multiple digits). On [ push and reset. On ] pop and set cur = prev + count * cur. Pitfall: reading only one digit.

fields.Question: Kth largest of n values, k much smaller than n. With heapq, which is O(n log k)?
fields.Choices:
Push all n values one by one into a max heap, then pop k times
Keep a max heap of size k
Sort and index
Keep a min heap of size k, pop when size exceeds k, answer is heap[0]
fields.Correct: Keep a min heap of size k, pop when size exceeds k, answer is heap[0]
fields.Explanation: A size k min heap keeps the k largest and its root is the kth largest. Pushing all n values one by one is O(n log n) before any pop. A size k max heap evicts the wrong items. Sorting is O(n log n).
fields.Hint: Which end of the heap do you evict?

fields.Question: What is the time to build a heap from n items with heapq.heapify?
fields.Choices:
O(n log n)
O(log n)
O(n^2)
O(n)
fields.Correct: O(n)
fields.Explanation: Bottom up heapify is linear because most nodes are near the leaves and sift down a short distance. O(n log n) is pushing n items one by one. O(log n) is one push. O(n^2) is insertion into a sorted list.

fields.Question: heapq.heappush(h, (dist, node)) where node is a custom object without ordering. When does it raise TypeError?
fields.Choices:
Only when dist is a float
When two entries have equal dist, Python compares the node objects
Always, tuples cannot be pushed
Never, heapq only compares the first element
fields.Correct: When two entries have equal dist, Python compares the node objects
fields.Explanation: Tuples compare element by element, so equal priorities fall through to the payload. Add a counter as a tie breaker: (dist, count, node). Tuples are pushable. heapq has no key argument and compares whole items. Float or int makes no difference.

fields.Question: On Python 3.13, heapq offers only min heap functions publicly. How do you get max heap behaviour for integers?
fields.Choices:
Sort the heap descending once
Push -x and negate when popping
Call the private heapq._heapify_max after every push
Push x and pop from h[-1]
fields.Correct: Push -x and negate when popping
fields.Explanation: Negation turns the min heap into a max heap. Private helpers are not a supported API and re-heapifying each push is O(n). Python 3.14 added public max heap functions, which is why the version is stated. h[-1] is not the max of a heap. Sorting once breaks on later pushes.

fields.Question: heapq.nlargest(k, iterable) on n items. What is the complexity a candidate should quote?
fields.Choices:
O(n log n)
O(k log n)
O(n k)
O(n log k)
fields.Correct: O(n log k)
fields.Explanation: nlargest keeps a heap of size k, so each of n items costs O(log k). O(n log n) is sorting. O(k log n) is heapify then k pops, which also needs O(n) to build. O(n k) is a linear scan per pick.

fields.Question: K Closest Points to Origin, n up to 10^4. Which is correct and avoids sqrt?
fields.Choices:
Compare sqrt(x*x + y*y) with a min heap of size k
Compare abs(x) + abs(y)
Sort by x then y
Compare x*x + y*y, keeping a size k max heap via negated distances
fields.Correct: Compare x*x + y*y, keeping a size k max heap via negated distances
fields.Explanation: Squared distance preserves order, and a size k max heap evicts the farthest. A size k min heap evicts the closest, which is backwards, and sqrt is unnecessary. Manhattan distance ranks differently from Euclidean. Sorting by coordinates is unrelated to distance.
fields.Source: LeetCode 973. K Closest Points to Origin (https://leetcode.com/problems/k-closest-points-to-origin/)

fields.Question:
Subsets with a shared path list. Output is a list of empty lists. Why?
def dfs(i):
    res.append(path)
    for j in range(i, len(nums)):
        path.append(nums[j]); dfs(j + 1); path.pop()
fields.Choices:
dfs should start from j instead of j + 1
path.pop() should come before dfs
res should be a set
It appends the same list object, so later pops empty every entry
fields.Correct: It appends the same list object, so later pops empty every entry
fields.Explanation: res holds references to one list that ends empty. Append path[:] or list(path). Starting from j allows reuse, a different problem. Popping before recursing drops the element. A set cannot hold lists and does not fix aliasing.

fields.Question: What is the time to generate all subsets of n distinct items, counting output?
fields.Correct: O(n 2^n)
fields.Explanation: There are 2^n subsets and copying each costs up to O(n). O(2^n) forgets the copy. O(n^2) is far too small. O(n!) is permutations.

fields.Question: Permutations of n distinct integers. How many leaves does the recursion tree have?
fields.Choices:
n^n
n^2
n!
2^n
fields.Correct: n!
fields.Explanation: Each level chooses one of the remaining items, so there are n! orderings. 2^n is subsets. n^n allows repeats. n^2 is pairs.

fields.Question: Combination Sum: unlimited reuse of distinct candidates, combinations must be unique. Which recursive call is right after choosing candidates[j]?
fields.Choices:
dfs(j + 1, remaining - candidates[j])
dfs(0, remaining - candidates[j])
dfs(i + 1, remaining - candidates[j])
dfs(j, remaining - candidates[j])
fields.Correct: dfs(j, remaining - candidates[j])
fields.Explanation: Passing j allows reuse of the same item while never going back, which keeps combinations unique. j + 1 forbids reuse. 0 produces permutations of the same combination. i + 1 ignores which item was chosen.

fields.Question: Subsets II with duplicates in nums. After sorting, which rule in the loop over j from i avoids ever generating a duplicate subset?
fields.Choices:
if nums[j] in path: continue
Skip nothing and dedupe res with a set of tuples at the end
if j > i and nums[j] == nums[j - 1]: continue
if j > 0 and nums[j] == nums[j - 1]: continue
fields.Correct: if j > i and nums[j] == nums[j - 1]: continue
fields.Explanation: Skipping only within the same level (j > i) avoids repeated branches while allowing a duplicate deeper in the path. j > 0 also skips at deeper levels and loses [2, 2]. Checking membership in path loses valid repeats. Final dedupe still generates every duplicate branch first, so it does not avoid generating them.

fields.Question: N-Queens: what three sets let you check a placement in O(1)?
fields.Answer: Columns, diagonals keyed by r - c, and anti diagonals keyed by r + c. Place one queen per row, add to the sets, recurse, then remove on backtrack.
fields.Hint: Diagonals have constant r - c or r + c.

fields.Question: Validate BST. A solution checks node.left.val < node.val < node.right.val at each node. Which tree breaks it?
fields.Choices:
5 with left 4 and right 6, where 6 has left child 3
5 with left 4 and right 6
A single node
An empty tree
fields.Correct: 5 with left 4 and right 6, where 6 has left child 3
fields.Explanation: Every local check passes but 3 sits in the right subtree of 5, violating the BST property. Pass lower and upper bounds down instead. The plain 5, 4, 6 tree is a valid BST and passes. A single node and an empty tree are valid.

fields.Question: Recursive max depth of a binary tree with n nodes. What is the worst case space?
fields.Choices:
O(log n)
O(1)
O(n log n)
O(n) for a skewed tree
fields.Correct: O(n) for a skewed tree
fields.Explanation: Recursion depth equals tree height, which is n for a linked list shaped tree. O(log n) holds only when balanced. Recursion is not O(1). No extra log factor applies.
fields.Hint: Height, not node count, in general.
fields.Source: LeetCode 104. Maximum Depth of Binary Tree (https://leetcode.com/problems/maximum-depth-of-binary-tree/)

fields.Question: Diameter of Binary Tree in edges. The helper returns height. What updates the answer at each node?
fields.Choices:
best = left_height + right_height at the root only
best = max(best, left_height * right_height)
best = max(best, left_height + right_height)
best = max(best, 1 + max(left_height, right_height))
fields.Correct: best = max(best, left_height + right_height)
fields.Explanation: The longest path through a node joins the two deepest branches. 1 + max is the height, not a path. Only checking the root misses paths that do not pass through it. Multiplying heights has no meaning.
fields.Hint: The path may not pass through the root.

fields.Question: Lowest Common Ancestor in a BST for p and q. Best time for a tree of height h?
fields.Choices:
O(n), search both paths and compare
O(log n) always
O(n log n)
O(h), walk down using values
fields.Correct: O(h), walk down using values
fields.Explanation: BST order says go left if both are smaller, right if both are larger, else stop. That is O(h). Comparing full paths is for general trees. O(log n) assumes balance. Nothing is sorted.
fields.Source: LeetCode 235. Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Search Tree (https://leetcode.com/problems/lowest-common-ancestor-of-a-binary-search-tree/)

fields.Question: Kth Smallest Element in a BST. Which traversal gives values in sorted order?
fields.Choices:
Inorder
Preorder
Postorder
Level order
fields.Correct: Inorder
fields.Explanation: Inorder visits left, node, right, which is ascending in a BST, so stop at the kth visit. Preorder and postorder do not sort. Level order visits by depth.
fields.Source: LeetCode 230. Kth Smallest Element in a BST (https://leetcode.com/problems/kth-smallest-element-in-a-bst/)

fields.Question: Same Tree: give the recursive check and its base cases.
fields.Answer: If both are None return True. If one is None or values differ return False. Otherwise return same(p.left, q.left) and same(p.right, q.right). O(n) time, O(h) stack.

fields.Question: Merge Intervals where intervals touching at an endpoint ([1,2] and [2,3]) count as overlapping. After sorting by start, when do you merge?
fields.Choices:
When start <= last start
When end <= last end
When start <= last end
When start < last end
fields.Correct: When start <= last end
fields.Explanation: Touching counts as overlap, so start equal to the last end merges. Strict less keeps [1,2] and [2,3] apart. Comparing to last start ignores ends. end <= last end only handles containment.

fields.Question: Merging [1,10] then [2,3]. Which update is right?
fields.Choices:
last[1] = cur[1]
last = cur
Append cur
last[1] = max(last[1], cur[1])
fields.Correct: last[1] = max(last[1], cur[1])
fields.Explanation: Containment means the new end may be smaller, so take the max. Assigning cur[1] shrinks [1,10] to [1,3]. Replacing last loses the start. Appending ignores the overlap.

fields.Question: Meeting Rooms: can one person attend all meetings, where a meeting ending at 10 and one starting at 10 do not conflict?
fields.Choices:
Sort by start and fail if any start < previous end
Sort by start and fail if any start <= previous end
Sort by end and fail if any end > next end
Check every pair
fields.Correct: Sort by start and fail if any start < previous end
fields.Explanation: Equal end and start is allowed, so only strict overlap fails. <= wrongly rejects back to back meetings. Comparing ends to ends misses overlaps. Every pair is O(n^2).

fields.Question: Non-overlapping Intervals: minimum removals. Which greedy is correct?
fields.Choices:
Remove the interval with the most overlaps repeatedly
Sort by end, keep each interval that starts at or after the last kept end
Sort by start, keep the first of each overlapping pair
Sort by length, keep shortest first
fields.Correct: Sort by end, keep each interval that starts at or after the last kept end
fields.Explanation: Keeping the earliest ending interval leaves the most room, the classic activity selection proof. Sorting by start keeps long early intervals that block many. Shortest first fails on cases where a short interval straddles two others. Max overlap removal is not proven optimal and is slow.

fields.Question: Insert Interval into a sorted, non overlapping list. Best time?
fields.Choices:
O(log n)
O(n^2)
O(n)
O(n log n)
fields.Correct: O(n)
fields.Explanation: One pass copies intervals before, merges the overlap and copies the rest. Re-sorting is unnecessary. Binary search finds the spot in O(log n) but the output still needs O(n). Repeated merging is not needed.

fields.Question: Climbing Stairs with 1 or 2 steps, n up to 45. Which runs in O(n) time and O(1) space?
fields.Choices:
Plain recursion f(n - 1) + f(n - 2)
Memoized recursion
A full dp array
Two rolling variables a, b = b, a + b
fields.Correct: Two rolling variables a, b = b, a + b
fields.Explanation: Each state needs only the previous two. Plain recursion is O(2^n). Memoization is O(n) time but O(n) space. A dp array is also O(n) space.

fields.Question: House Robber recurrence for dp[i], the best up to house i?
fields.Choices:
dp[i] = max(dp[i - 1], nums[i])
Take every other house, odd or even, whichever is larger
dp[i] = max(dp[i - 1], dp[i - 2] + nums[i])
dp[i] = dp[i - 2] + nums[i]
fields.Correct: dp[i] = max(dp[i - 1], dp[i - 2] + nums[i])
fields.Explanation: Either skip house i or take it with the best up to i - 2. Always taking i forces a choice. max(dp[i - 1], nums[i]) forgets the sum. Alternating fails on [2, 1, 1, 2] where the best is 4 from houses 0 and 3.

fields.Question: Coin Change: coins = [1, 3, 4], amount = 6, fewest coins. What does largest coin first greedy return, and what is optimal?
fields.Choices:
Greedy 2, optimal 2
Greedy 3, optimal 3
Greedy fails to find any answer
Greedy 3 coins (4, 1, 1), optimal 2 (3, 3)
fields.Correct: Greedy 3 coins (4, 1, 1), optimal 2 (3, 3)
fields.Explanation: Greedy takes 4 then two 1s. DP finds 3 + 3. Greedy is only optimal for canonical coin systems. It does find an answer because 1 exists.

fields.Question:
Coin Change II counts combinations. Which loop order counts each combination once?
dp = [1] + [0] * amount
# loops here
    dp[a] += dp[a - c]
fields.Correct: for c in coins: for a in range(c, amount + 1)
fields.Explanation: Coins outer means each combination is built in coin order, so it is counted once. Amount outer counts ordered sequences (permutations), which is Combination Sum IV. Iterating amounts downward is 0/1 knapsack, so each coin is used at most once. The orders differ: for amount 3 with coins 1 and 2 they give 2 and 3.
fields.Hint: Outer loop fixes the order of choices.

fields.Question: 0/1 knapsack with a 1D dp over capacity. Why iterate capacity from high to low?
fields.Choices:
It does not matter
So dp[w - weight] still holds the value without the current item, preventing reuse
For cache locality
Because low to high overflows
fields.Correct: So dp[w - weight] still holds the value without the current item, preventing reuse
fields.Explanation: Going downward reads states from the previous item row. Going upward lets an item be added multiple times, which is unbounded knapsack. Cache locality is not the reason. Overflow is unrelated. It matters for correctness.

fields.Question: Longest Increasing Subsequence in O(n log n) with a tails array. For each x, what happens?
fields.Choices:
Insert x in sorted position
Replace tails[bisect_left(tails, x)] with x, or append if at the end
Replace tails[bisect_right(tails, x)], or append
Append x if larger than tails[-1], else ignore
fields.Correct: Replace tails[bisect_left(tails, x)] with x, or append if at the end
fields.Explanation: bisect_left keeps strict increase: an equal value replaces rather than extends. bisect_right counts non decreasing sequences. Ignoring smaller x loses better tails. Inserting grows the array beyond the LIS length.

fields.Question: Edit Distance dp[i][j] for word1[:i] and word2[:j]. When word1[i - 1] != word2[j - 1], what is dp[i][j]?
fields.Explanation: Delete, insert and replace each cost 1. Only replace ignores insert and delete. Adding 2 models delete plus insert in place of replace, the LCS style distance. max is wrong for a minimum.

fields.Question: Word Break with memo on start index, string length n, dictionary of words up to length L stored in a set. For each start you try every end up to n and slice. What is the time?
fields.Choices:
O(n^2)
O(2^n)
O(n^3): n states, n ends, O(n) slice and hash
O(n): one per state
fields.Correct: O(n^3): n states, n ends, O(n) slice and hash
fields.Explanation: Memoization caps states at n, but each tries up to n ends and slicing plus hashing costs O(n), giving O(n^3), or O(n^2 L) if ends are capped at L. O(n) counts states only. O(n^2) forgets the slice cost. O(2^n) is without memoization.

fields.Question: Longest Common Subsequence of lengths m and n. Minimum space while still returning the length?
fields.Choices:
O(m n)
O(1)
O(m + n)
O(min(m, n)) with two rolling rows
fields.Correct: O(min(m, n)) with two rolling rows
fields.Explanation: Each row depends only on the previous row, so keep two rows of the shorter length. O(m n) is the full table, needed only to reconstruct the sequence directly. O(1) cannot hold the dependencies. O(m + n) is more than needed.
fields.Hint: Row i needs only row i - 1.

fields.Question: Unique Paths II on a grid with obstacles. In the first row, what is dp[0][j] after an obstacle at (0, 2)?
fields.Choices:
1 for every j except j = 2
0 only at j = 2
Undefined, first row is not filled
0 for every j >= 2
fields.Correct: 0 for every j >= 2
fields.Explanation: A path along the first row cannot pass the obstacle, so everything to its right is 0. Initializing the whole row to 1 is the classic bug. Only zeroing j = 2 still lets j = 3 inherit 1. The first row is filled as a base case.

fields.Question: Partition Equal Subset Sum, n up to 200, values up to 100. Which state works?
fields.Choices:
dp over indices only
Greedy: sort descending and fill the smaller side
Backtracking over all subsets
Boolean dp over sums up to total / 2, 0/1 knapsack style
fields.Correct: Boolean dp over sums up to total / 2, 0/1 knapsack style
fields.Explanation: Target is total / 2 at most 10^4, so a sum indexed boolean dp is O(n target). Indices alone do not capture reachable sums. The greedy fails on [3, 3, 2, 2, 2]. Brute force is 2^200.

fields.Question: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock with Cooldown. What is the minimal state set per day?
fields.Choices:
held, sold today, rested (not holding, free to buy)
held and not held
profit only
day index and number of transactions
fields.Correct: held, sold today, rested (not holding, free to buy)
fields.Explanation: Cooldown means the day after selling you cannot buy, so not holding must split into just sold and rested. Two states let you buy right after selling. Profit alone loses holding status. Transactions are unlimited here, so counting them is unneeded.
fields.Source: LeetCode 309. Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock with Cooldown (https://leetcode.com/problems/best-time-to-buy-and-sell-stock-with-cooldown/)

fields.Question: Decode Ways for s = "10" and s = "06". What should a correct dp return?
fields.Choices:
2 and 0
1 and 0
2 and 1
1 and 1
fields.Correct: 1 and 0
fields.Explanation: "10" is only J, and "06" has no valid decoding because a leading 0 is invalid. 2 for "10" counts "1","0", but 0 alone is not a letter. 1 for "06" accepts 6 after an invalid 0.

fields.Question: Burst Balloons: why define dp[i][j] by the last balloon burst in (i, j) rather than the first?
fields.Answer: If k is the last burst in (i, j), its neighbours at that moment are the fixed boundaries i and j, so the subproblems (i, k) and (k, j) are independent: dp[i][j] = max over k of dp[i][k] + nums[i] nums[k] nums[j] + dp[k][j]. Choosing the first burst makes neighbours depend on later choices. O(n^3).

fields.Question: Koko Eating Bananas, n piles up to 10^4, pile sizes up to 10^9. Binary search on speed. What is the total time?
fields.Choices:
O(n log M) where M is the max pile
O(log M)
O(n log n)
O(M n)
fields.Correct: O(n log M) where M is the max pile
fields.Explanation: Each candidate speed costs an O(n) feasibility check, and there are O(log M) candidates. O(log M) forgets the check. O(n log n) is sorting. O(M n) is trying every speed.

fields.Question: Koko hours for pile p at speed k. Which is right with integers?
fields.Explanation: Ceiling division counts a partial hour. p // k undercounts. p / k is a float. p // k + 1 overcounts when k divides p.

fields.Question: Capacity To Ship Packages Within D Days. What are the search bounds for capacity?
fields.Choices:
lo = max(weights), hi = sum(weights)
lo = 1, hi = max(weights)
lo = min(weights), hi = max(weights)
lo = sum(weights) // D, hi = max(weights)
fields.Correct: lo = max(weights), hi = sum(weights)
fields.Explanation: Capacity must carry the heaviest package and never needs more than all in one day. hi = max(weights) is too small when D is small. min is not a valid lower bound. sum // D can be below the heaviest package and the upper bound is wrong.
fields.Source: LeetCode 1011. Capacity To Ship Packages Within D Days (https://leetcode.com/problems/capacity-to-ship-packages-within-d-days/)

fields.Question: When is binary search on the answer valid?
fields.Choices:
When the input array is sorted
When the answer is an integer
When the cost function is convex
When feasibility is monotone: if x works then every larger x works (or every smaller)
fields.Correct: When feasibility is monotone: if x works then every larger x works (or every smaller)
fields.Explanation: You need a predicate that flips once. Sorted input is not required, for example shipping weights stay in order. Integer answers alone do not give monotonicity. Convexity is ternary search territory.

fields.Question: Median of Two Sorted Arrays of sizes m and n. Which array do you binary search and what is the time?
fields.Choices:
The shorter one, O(log min(m, n))
The longer one, O(log max(m, n))
Both merged, O(m + n)
Both alternately, O(log m + log n)
fields.Correct: The shorter one, O(log min(m, n))
fields.Explanation: Partitioning the shorter array keeps the other partition index in range and gives O(log min). Searching the longer can produce invalid partitions. Merging is O(m + n), not logarithmic. Alternating has no clean invariant.
fields.Source: LeetCode 4. Median of Two Sorted Arrays (https://leetcode.com/problems/median-of-two-sorted-arrays/)

fields.Question: Split Array Largest Sum into k parts: give the binary search on answer.
fields.Answer: Search the max part sum between max(nums) and sum(nums). For a candidate cap, greedily count parts by starting a new part when the running sum would exceed it. If parts <= k the cap is feasible, move hi down, else lo up. O(n log(sum)). Requires non negative values.

fields.Question: Kahn's topological sort on Course Schedule II. How do you detect a cycle?
fields.Choices:
The output has fewer than n nodes
The queue becomes empty
Some node has indegree 0 at the start
A node is visited twice
fields.Correct: The output has fewer than n nodes
fields.Explanation: Nodes on a cycle never reach indegree 0, so they are never output. The queue always empties eventually. Indegree 0 at the start is normal. Kahn's never visits a node twice by construction.

fields.Question: Cycle detection in a directed graph with DFS. Why is a single visited set not enough?
fields.Choices:
A node visited in an earlier finished branch is not a back edge; you need in progress and done states
It is enough
Because DFS must be iterative
Because undirected and directed are the same
fields.Correct: A node visited in an earlier finished branch is not a back edge; you need in progress and done states
fields.Explanation: Cross edges to finished nodes look like revisits but are not cycles. Three colors mark on stack nodes. A single set gives false positives on diamonds. Recursion is fine. Directed and undirected cycle rules differ.

fields.Question: Course Schedule: prerequisites [a, b] means take b before a. For Kahn's, which edge and indegree?
fields.Choices:
Edge a to b, indegree[b] += 1
Edge a to b, indegree[a] += 1
Both directions
Edge b to a, indegree[a] += 1
fields.Correct: Edge b to a, indegree[a] += 1
fields.Explanation: b must come first, so b points to a and a waits. Reversing the edge returns the reverse order, which is wrong for Course Schedule II. Mixing directions breaks the counts. Both directions turns every edge into a cycle.

fields.Question: Alien Dictionary: words ["abc", "ab"]. What is the answer?
fields.Choices:
Any order of a, b, c
Invalid, return "" because a word precedes its own prefix
"abc"
"cba"
fields.Correct: Invalid, return "" because a word precedes its own prefix
fields.Explanation: A longer word cannot come before its prefix in a sorted list, so the input is inconsistent. Returning a letter order ignores that check, a frequent miss.

fields.Question: Is Graph Bipartite, graph may be disconnected. What is commonly missed?
fields.Choices:
Starting a BFS coloring from every uncolored node, not just node 0
Coloring with three colors
Checking for self loops only
Sorting the adjacency lists
fields.Correct: Starting a BFS coloring from every uncolored node, not just node 0
fields.Explanation: A component never reached from node 0 can contain an odd cycle. Bipartite means two colors. Self loops are one case of odd cycles, not the whole check. Sorting is irrelevant.

fields.Question: Shortest Path in a Grid with Obstacles Elimination (up to k removals). What is the BFS state?
fields.Choices:
(removals used)
(row, col, removals used)
(row, col)
(row, col, steps)
fields.Correct: (row, col, removals used)
fields.Explanation: Reaching a cell with fewer removals left is a different state. Visited by cell only prunes paths that would succeed. Steps are the BFS level, not part of identity. Removals alone forget position.
fields.Source: LeetCode 1293. Shortest Path in a Grid with Obstacles Elimination (https://leetcode.com/problems/shortest-path-in-a-grid-with-obstacles-elimination/)

fields.Question: Evaluate Division: a / b = 2.0, b / c = 3.0, query a / c. How do you model it?
fields.Choices:
Unweighted graph, count hops
Sort variables
Union find without weights
Weighted directed graph with edges a to b weight 2 and b to a weight 0.5, multiply along a path
fields.Correct: Weighted directed graph with edges a to b weight 2 and b to a weight 0.5, multiply along a path
fields.Explanation: Ratios multiply along paths and reverse edges invert. Hop counts lose values. Sorting has no meaning. Plain union find tells connectivity but not the ratio; it needs weights.

fields.Question: Reconstruct Itinerary using all tickets with the smallest lexical order. Approach?
fields.Answer: Eulerian path with Hierholzer's algorithm: adjacency lists sorted (or min heaps), DFS popping the smallest destination, append the airport after its edges are exhausted, then reverse. Plain greedy smallest next can dead end.

fields.Question: Shortest paths with some negative edge weights and no negative cycles. Which is correct?
fields.Choices:
Dijkstra with a binary heap
BFS
Dijkstra after adding a constant to every edge
Bellman Ford
fields.Correct: Bellman Ford
fields.Explanation: Bellman Ford relaxes all edges V - 1 times and handles negatives. Dijkstra finalizes nodes early and can be wrong. BFS ignores weights. Adding a constant penalizes paths with more edges and changes which path is shortest.

fields.Question: Lazy Dijkstra with heapq. When you pop (d, u) and d > dist[u], what do you do?
fields.Choices:
Skip it, it is a stale entry
Relax its neighbours anyway
Update dist[u] = d
Stop the algorithm
fields.Correct: Skip it, it is a stale entry
fields.Explanation: heapq has no decrease key, so old entries remain and must be skipped. Relaxing from stale entries wastes work. Setting dist to a larger value is wrong. Stopping ends early.

fields.Question: Union find without path compression or union by rank on n elements. Worst case per find?
fields.Choices:
Nearly O(1), inverse Ackermann
O(log n)
O(1)
O(n)
fields.Correct: O(n)
fields.Explanation: Unions can build a chain, so find walks n links. Inverse Ackermann needs both optimizations. O(log n) needs union by rank or size. O(1) is never guaranteed.

fields.Question: Redundant Connection in an undirected graph: which edge to return?
fields.Choices:
Any edge on the cycle
The edge with the largest node
The first edge whose endpoints already share a root
The last edge in the input
fields.Correct: The first edge whose endpoints already share a root
fields.Explanation: Processing edges in order, the first edge whose endpoints are already connected closes the only cycle, and it is the cycle edge that appears last in the input, which is what the problem asks for. The literal last input edge may not lie on the cycle. Any cycle edge is not unique, the problem wants the last one. Node labels are irrelevant.

fields.Question: Number of connected components with union find over n nodes and m edges. How do you get the count?
fields.Choices:
n - m
Start at n and decrement on each successful union
Count distinct parent[i] values without calling find
Count edges
fields.Correct: Start at n and decrement on each successful union
fields.Explanation: Each union of distinct sets merges two components. parent entries may not be roots without find. Edge count says nothing directly. n - m is wrong when edges are redundant.
fields.Source: LeetCode 323. Number of Connected Components in an Undirected Graph (https://leetcode.com/problems/number-of-connected-components-in-an-undirected-graph/)

fields.Question: Accounts Merge: what do you union?
fields.Choices:
Accounts in input order
Emails within the same account, then group emails by root
Account names
All accounts with any shared letters
fields.Correct: Emails within the same account, then group emails by root
fields.Explanation: Emails identify people, so emails in one account join and shared emails join accounts. Names collide across different people. Letters are meaningless. Input order is arbitrary.

fields.Question: Many prefix queries (startsWith) over a large word list. Why a trie instead of a hash set of words?
fields.Choices:
Hash sets cannot store strings
Tries sort the words
A prefix check costs O(L) regardless of how many words share it
Tries use less memory than sets
fields.Correct: A prefix check costs O(L) regardless of how many words share it
fields.Explanation: A trie walks L nodes for a prefix of length L. A set would need every prefix stored or a scan. Tries usually use more memory because of per node maps. Sets store strings fine. Ordered traversal is a side effect, not the reason.

fields.Question: Trie insert("apple"), then search("app") returns True. What is the bug?
fields.Choices:
search checks only that the path exists, not an end of word flag
insert skips the last character
The root should store a character
Children should be a list
fields.Correct: search checks only that the path exists, not an end of word flag
fields.Explanation: A path for app exists inside apple, so search must check is_end at the final node. Skipping a character would fail other cases. The root holds no character by design. A list or dict for children is an implementation detail.

fields.Question: Word Search II: board m x n, many words. Why build a trie of words instead of running Word Search per word?
fields.Choices:
It avoids the visited marking
It is required to handle diagonal moves
One DFS per cell explores all words sharing a prefix and prunes when no word continues
It makes each DFS O(1)
fields.Correct: One DFS per cell explores all words sharing a prefix and prunes when no word continues
fields.Explanation: The trie shares prefix work across words and stops paths no word can follow. DFS is not O(1). Visited marking is still needed. Moves are not diagonal.

fields.Question: Design Add and Search Words where '.' matches any letter. What does search do on '.'?
fields.Choices:
Fail immediately
Recurse into every child at that level
Skip the character
Match only child 'a'
fields.Correct: Recurse into every child at that level
fields.Explanation: A wildcard can be any letter, so try each child. Skipping shifts the remaining pattern. Picking one child misses matches. Failing ignores the wildcard.
fields.Source: LeetCode 211. Design Add and Search Words Data Structure (https://leetcode.com/problems/design-add-and-search-words-data-structure/)

fields.Question: Largest Rectangle in Histogram with a monotonic increasing stack of indices. When you pop index i at current index r, what is the width?
fields.Choices:
i - stack[-1]
r - stack[-1] - 1 after popping, or r if the stack is empty
r - i
r - i + 1
fields.Correct: r - stack[-1] - 1 after popping, or r if the stack is empty
fields.Explanation: Bar i extends from just after the new top to just before r. r - i misses the left extension. r - i + 1 includes r, which is shorter. i - stack[-1] measures only the left side.
fields.Hint: Left boundary is the new top.

fields.Question: Largest Rectangle in Histogram. Why append a 0 height at the end?
fields.Choices:
It forces every remaining bar to be popped and measured
It handles negative heights
It avoids an empty stack check entirely
It makes the stack decreasing
fields.Correct: It forces every remaining bar to be popped and measured
fields.Explanation: Bars still on the stack at the end are never measured without a final flush. Heights are non negative. You still need the empty stack case for width. The stack stays increasing.

fields.Question: Next Greater Element II on a circular array of n. How do you handle wraparound?
fields.Choices:
Concatenate the array with itself and return the answers for all 2n
Run the stack twice independently
Sort the array
Iterate i from 0 to 2n - 1 using i % n, pushing only in the first pass
fields.Correct: Iterate i from 0 to 2n - 1 using i % n, pushing only in the first pass
fields.Explanation: A second pass resolves elements whose greater value is before them, and only n results are kept. Returning 2n answers is the wrong size. Two independent runs lose the pending stack. Sorting loses positions.

fields.Question: A monotonic stack loop has a while pop inside a for loop. Why is it O(n) and not O(n^2)?
fields.Choices:
The while loop runs at most once per iteration
The stack has at most log n items
Because the input is sorted
Each index is pushed once and popped at most once
fields.Correct: Each index is pushed once and popped at most once
fields.Explanation: Total pops cannot exceed total pushes, so the while body runs at most n times overall. A single iteration can pop many. The stack can hold n items. Input need not be sorted.

fields.Question: Merge k sorted lists with N total nodes using a heap of list heads. Time?
fields.Choices:
O(N log k)
O(N log N)
O(N k)
O(k log N)
fields.Correct: O(N log k)
fields.Explanation: The heap holds at most k items and each of N nodes is pushed and popped once. O(N log N) is collecting then sorting. O(N k) is scanning all heads each step. O(k log N) undercounts.

fields.Question: Find Median from Data Stream with two heaps. Invariant?
fields.Choices:
Two min heaps of equal size
A max heap of the upper half
One sorted list with bisect.insort
Max heap of the lower half, min heap of the upper half, sizes differ by at most 1
fields.Correct: Max heap of the lower half, min heap of the upper half, sizes differ by at most 1
fields.Explanation: The tops of the two halves give the median in O(1) and inserts are O(log n). Two min heaps cannot expose the lower half's max. A max heap of the upper half exposes the wrong end. insort is O(n) per insert due to shifting.
fields.Source: LeetCode 295. Find Median from Data Stream (https://leetcode.com/problems/find-median-from-data-stream/)

fields.Question: Task Scheduler with cooldown n. Tasks A x3, B x3, n = 2. Minimum intervals?
fields.Explanation: (max_count - 1) * (n + 1) + count_of_max = 2 * 3 + 2 = 8: A B idle A B idle A B. 6 ignores cooldown. 7 counts only one task at the end. 9 adds an extra idle.

fields.Question: IPO: pick at most k projects to maximize capital. Which structure combination?
fields.Choices:
A single max heap of profits
Sort by profit descending and take the first k affordable
DP over capital
Projects sorted by capital needed, plus a max heap of profits for affordable ones
fields.Correct: Projects sorted by capital needed, plus a max heap of profits for affordable ones
fields.Explanation: Unlock affordable projects as capital grows and always take the best profit. A profit only heap includes unaffordable projects. Sorting by profit once ignores that capital grows. DP over capital up to 10^9 is infeasible.

fields.Question: Jump Game: can you reach the last index? Which O(n) rule is correct?
fields.Choices:
Track the furthest reachable index and fail if i exceeds it
Always jump the maximum length
DP over all jumps from each index
Recursively try every jump length from each index
fields.Correct: Track the furthest reachable index and fail if i exceeds it
fields.Explanation: The furthest reach invariant proves reachability. Max jumps can land on a 0 and miss a better shorter jump. DP is O(n^2), not O(n). Unmemoized recursion is exponential.

fields.Question: Gas Station: if total gas >= total cost, where do you start?
fields.Choices:
Index 0
The station with the most gas
The station with the largest gas - cost
The index after the last point where the running tank went negative
fields.Correct: The index after the last point where the running tank went negative
fields.Explanation: If you fail from s to j, no station between them can work, so restart after j; the total check guarantees that start succeeds. Index 0 can fail. Most gas or best single gain ignores the route.
fields.Hint: Failing segments rule out their starts.

fields.Question: How does an exchange argument prove a greedy choice?
fields.Choices:
Show it is locally optimal at each step
Show it runs in O(n log n)
Show any optimal solution can be changed to include the greedy choice without getting worse
Test it on many random inputs
fields.Correct: Show any optimal solution can be changed to include the greedy choice without getting worse
fields.Explanation: Exchange arguments transform an optimal solution step by step into the greedy one. Random tests are not proof. Local optimality alone is the claim, not the proof. Runtime says nothing about correctness.

fields.Question: Partition Labels: what drives the cut points?
fields.Choices:
The last index of each character; cut when i equals the max last index seen
First index of each character
Character frequency
Cut on every repeated character
fields.Correct: The last index of each character; cut when i equals the max last index seen
fields.Explanation: Extend the current part to the furthest last occurrence of any letter in it, and cut when you reach it. First indexes do not bound a part. Frequencies ignore position. Cutting on repeats splits letters across parts.

fields.Question: Meeting Rooms II: minimum rooms. Which is O(n log n)?
fields.Choices:
Count the max meetings that start at the same time
Merge intervals and count merged groups
Sort by start, min heap of end times, pop while the top end <= current start
Sort by start and count overlaps with the previous meeting only
fields.Correct: Sort by start, min heap of end times, pop while the top end <= current start
fields.Explanation: The heap holds rooms in use, and its max size is the answer. Comparing only adjacent meetings misses three way overlaps. Same start counts ignore overlaps with different starts. Merging gives busy blocks, not concurrency.

fields.Question: Sweep line for max concurrent meetings with events (time, +1) and (time, -1), half open intervals [start, end). How should ties sort?
fields.Choices:
End events (-1) before start events (+1) at the same time
Start events before end events
Ties do not matter
By meeting length
fields.Correct: End events (-1) before start events (+1) at the same time
fields.Explanation: With half open intervals a meeting ending at t frees the room for one starting at t, so -1 first. Starts first overcounts back to back meetings. Ties change the max. Length is irrelevant.

fields.Question: LRU Cache with O(1) get and put. Which structure?
fields.Choices:
An array sorted by last access
Hash map from key to node in a doubly linked list ordered by recency
Hash map plus a min heap of timestamps
Hash map plus a singly linked list
fields.Correct: Hash map from key to node in a doubly linked list ordered by recency
fields.Explanation: The map finds the node and the doubly linked list unlinks and moves it in O(1). A heap makes updates O(log n) with stale entries. A singly linked list cannot remove a node without its predecessor in O(1). A sorted array is O(n) per access.

fields.Question: An LRU cache passes put tests but evicts the wrong key after get(k). What is the likely bug?
fields.Choices:
